title: Sāṃkhya Kārikā

attribution.tradition: Composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa, who summarized in āryā verses the doctrine handed down from the supreme sage (Kapila) through Āsuri and Pañcaśikha by a succession of pupils (SK 70–71); its topics are those of the whole Ṣaṣṭitantra (SK 72).
attribution.scholarly: Authorship accepted. Verses 70–72 are not commented on by Gauḍapāda; Paramārtha's Chinese version lacks v. 63 and its commentary remarks that v. 72 is not original; a 73rd verse is found only in the Māṭhara Vṛtti and in one anonymous vṛtti (V1).

scholarly.text: c. 350–450 CE (before Paramārtha's Chinese translation, c. 557–569 CE)

structure.description: 72 āryā verses in the vulgate (69 doctrinal verses and 3 on the transmission); some versions add a 73rd; 'saptati' (seventy) is a round name

summary: The classical root text of Sāṃkhya. Starting from the threefold suffering and the inadequacy of seen and Vedic remedies, it sets out the three means of knowledge, the pre-existence of the effect, the manifest and the unmanifest, the three guṇas, the proofs of prakṛti and of many puruṣas, the emergence of the twenty-five principles, the thirteen instruments and the subtle body, the fifty-fold creation of cognitions, and liberation (kaivalya) through the knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I'.

editions.name: F. Ruzsa's GRETIL e-text (1998) with variants from Solomon's V1/V2, Takakusu's study of the Chinese version, Gauḍapāda, the Yuktidīpikā, Māṭhara and the Jayamaṅgalā
H. H. Wilson, The Sāṅkhya Kārikā with the Bhāṣya of Gauḍapāda (Oxford 1837)

notes: Verse numbers and wording used in this unit's SK teachings were checked against the local GRETIL/DCS e-texts in sources_raw/; entries stay at skeleton level until Phase C/D.

title: Sāṃkhyakārikābhāṣya of Gauḍapāda

attribution.tradition: Ascribed to Gauḍapāda in its closing verse ('bhāṣyaṃ cātra gauḍapādakṛtam').
attribution.scholarly: Whether this Gauḍapāda is the Advaita teacher of the Māṇḍūkya-kārikā (Śaṅkara's paramaguru) is disputed and doubted by many scholars; the commentary is closely related to the commentary preserved in Paramārtha's Chinese version.

scholarly.text: uncertain; often placed c. 6th–8th c. CE

structure.description: comments on SK 1–69 only; vv. 70–72 are left uncommented

summary: A concise commentary on SK 1–69. It presents Kapila as one of Brahmā's seven mind-born sons, born with virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power, who taught the twenty-five principles to Āsuri; names the three kinds of suffering; explains dharma through compassion, giving and the Pātañjala yamas and niyamas; lists the eight powers; details the fifty categories of the creation of cognitions; and argues that neither Īśvara, nature (svabhāva) nor time, but prakṛti, is the world's cause.

editions.name: Wilson 1837 (Bombay reprint 1887), GRETIL e-text (input D. Patel), kārikās arranged after T. G. Mainkar (1972)

title: Māṭharavṛtti

attribution.scholarly: Date and relation to the commentary in Paramārtha's Chinese version are disputed: some have held it the source of that commentary, others place it several centuries later.

scholarly.text: disputed (proposals range from before the 6th c. to c. 1000 CE)

structure.description: commentary on 73 verses, including the extra 73rd verse

summary: A vṛtti on the SK that opens with the story of Kapila — an avatāra of the primal Person, son of Kardama and Devahūti — testing the brahmin Āsuri at thousand-year intervals before accepting him; it traces the teaching from Pañcaśikha through Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta and Devala to Īśvarakṛṣṇa, and enumerates the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra.

editions.name: Viṣṇu Prasāda Śarmā (ed.), Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series 296 [56], Varanasi 1970; GRETIL/DCS e-text

title: Yuktidīpikā

attribution.tradition: A colophon in the edition names Vācaspati Miśra ('kṛtir iyaṃ śrīvācaspatimiśrāṇām').
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; the colophon ascription to Vācaspati Miśra is not accepted.

structure.description: introductory verses and a commentary on the SK in four prakaraṇas and eleven āhnikas

summary: The most extensive old commentary on the SK. It defends Sāṃkhya against rival schools, preserves the divergent views of earlier Sāṃkhya teachers (Vārṣagaṇya, Vindhyavāsin, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Paurika, the Sāṃkhya teacher Patañjali), enumerates the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra and gives a list of teachers between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa.

editions.name: Shiv Kumar & D. N. Bhargava (eds.), 2 vols., Delhi 1990–92; GRETIL/DCS e-text

title: Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī

scholarly.text: 9th or 10th c. CE (Vācaspati's date is disputed: 841 or 976 CE, depending on the era of the date in his Nyāyasūcīnibandha)

summary: Vācaspati Miśra's commentary, the standard Sāṃkhya text of later tradition. It defines the three kinds of suffering; defends the impurity of sacrificial killing with a saying of Pañcaśikha; describes the path from hearing scripture through reasoning to long, uninterrupted, reverent practice ending in the knowledge 'I am not'; classifies inference; reduces other proposed means of knowledge to three; and explains how buddhi, taking on the reflection of consciousness, appears conscious.

editions.name: DCS (Digital Corpus of Sanskrit) partial text, on SK 1–15

notes: Only the part on SK 1–15 was available locally; teachings on later verses are from memory (low confidence).

title: Jayamaṅgalā

attribution.tradition: Its colophon ascribes it to Śaṅkara Bhagavat, pupil of Govinda Bhagavatpāda.
attribution.scholarly: The ascription to (Ādi) Śaṅkara is doubted; the opening salutation to a sage 'who teaches the supramundane' (lokottaravādin) has been read as pointing to another author.

summary: A commentary on the Sāṃkhyasaptati: liberation comes from knowing the twenty-five principles; the Saptati was written because the Ṣaṣṭitantra is too extensive; it quotes the verse that the knower of the twenty-five principles is liberated in whatever stage of life.

editions.name: H. Sarma (ed.), Calcutta Oriental Series 19, Calcutta 1926; GRETIL/DCS e-text

title: Jin qishi lun

attribution.scholarly: The kārikās with a commentary closely related to Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya and the Māṭhara Vṛtti; it lacks SK 63, and its commentary remarks that SK 72 is not original (as reported in the apparatus of Ruzsa's GRETIL edition, after Takakusu 1904).

summary: Paramārtha's Chinese translation of the Sāṃkhya Kārikā with a commentary — the earliest datable witness to the SK, fixing its latest date; it preserves a line of teachers and variant readings.

title: Ṣaṣṭitantra

attribution.tradition: The extensive doctrine (tantra) of the supreme sage, of which the SK is a condensation (SK 72; Yuktidīpikā introductory verses; Jayamaṅgalā on SK 1).
attribution.scholarly: Lost. Authorship proposals include Pañcaśikha and Vārṣagaṇya; some have taken 'ṣaṣṭitantra' as a name of the system rather than of a single book.

structure.description: sixty topics: ten fundamental topics (mūlikārtha) and the fifty categories of the creation of cognitions (5 errors, 28 incapacities, 9 contentments, 8 accomplishments)

summary: The lost 'doctrine of sixty topics' that the SK claims to summarize without its illustrative tales and polemics (SK 72). The later commentaries list its sixty topics; the Pāñcarātra Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā (ch. 12) gives a different, theistic account of a Kāpila Ṣaṣṭitantra.
notes: Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā chapter reference from memory (low confidence).

title: Rājavārttika (Sāṃkhya)

attribution.scholarly: Lost work quoted by Vācaspati Miśra (Tattvakaumudī on SK 72) for the verses enumerating the sixty topics; author unknown.

summary: A lost Sāṃkhya work known from Vācaspati Miśra's quotation of its verses listing the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra (ten fundamental topics and the fifty).
notes: Quotation recalled from the Tattvakaumudī on SK 72 (not in the local partial text).

title: Pañcaśikha fragments (Pañcaśikhasūtra)

attribution.scholarly: Prose sayings preserved as quotations, chiefly in the Yoga Bhāṣya (e.g., on YS 1.4, 1.25, 1.36, 2.13), where Vācaspati Miśra identifies them as Pañcaśikha's; collected in modern editions (e.g., N. Sinha, The Sāṃkhya Philosophy, 1915).

summary: Fragments ascribed to Pañcaśikha: that discrimination (khyāti) is the one 'seeing'; that the first knower, assuming a created mind, taught the doctrine to Āsuri out of compassion; that one should know the self as atomic ('I am'); and that the merit of sacrifice carries a slight, removable admixture of demerit.

title: Sāṃkhya Sūtra

attribution.scholarly: A late compilation, usually dated 14th–15th c. CE; it is first commented on by Aniruddha (c. 1500), and scholars note that older doxographies treat Sāṃkhya only through the Kārikā.

tradition.text: Kapila, the first knower (the tradition's account)

structure.description: six books: (1) the topics of the system, (2) the products of prakṛti, (3) the non-specific and specific, bodies, the path and liberation while living, (4) illustrative tales (ākhyāyikā), (5) refutation of rival views, (6) summary. 526 sūtras in the Sansknet e-text (164, 47, 85, 32, 129, 69); counts differ slightly between recensions

summary: The sūtra text of later Sāṃkhya. It restates the Kārikā's system, supplies the illustrative tales the Kārikā omitted, and argues at length against rivals: that Īśvara is not established as creator, that bondage is not due to avidyā, that things are not momentary, that consciousness is not a product of the elements, that the Veda is neither eternal nor authored yet self-valid; it accepts liberation while living and explains meditation as the removal of passion.

title: Sāṃkhyasūtravṛtti of Aniruddha
summary: The earliest known commentary on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, a brief vṛtti generally read as keeping to the sūtras' non-theistic position.
notes: Characterization of its position on Īśvara is recalled, not checked.

title: Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya
summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's extensive commentary on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, reading Sāṃkhya as compatible with a theistic Vedānta: the sūtras' denial that Īśvara is established is treated as a concessive argument, and Sāṃkhya is presented as the discipline of discrimination within a wider scriptural whole.

editions.name: R. Garbe (ed.), Harvard Oriental Series 2 (2nd ed. 1943)

title: Laghusāṃkhyasūtravṛtti

title: Sāṃkhyasāra

structure.description: two parts (pūrvabhāga, uttarabhāga) divided into paricchedas; verse and prose

summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's manual of Sāṃkhya, written to supply what the Kārikā left unsaid and to summarize his Sāṃkhya Bhāṣya; it opens by saluting Viṣṇu as the Lord, the self-born 'sprout of the world' called mahat, and presents liberation as the direct realization of the discrimination of self and non-self.

title: Tattvasamāsa

attribution.tradition: Aphorisms of Kapila, taught to a brahmin afflicted by the threefold suffering.
attribution.scholarly: Date uncertain: some regard its content as archaic, most place the text late; commentators divide it into 22–25 sūtras.

structure.description: 25 sūtras in Ṣimānanda's division (23 in the Kramadīpikā's): eight prakṛtis, sixteen modifications, puruṣa, the three guṇas, emergence and dissolution, adhyātma/adhibhūta/adhidaiva, the fives, the five-jointed avidyā, incapacity, contentment, accomplishment, the ten fundamental topics, creations, threefold bondage, liberation, means of knowledge and suffering

summary: A very brief list of the Sāṃkhya topics in aphorisms, the basis of several late commentaries.

editions.name: V. P. Dvivedin (ed.), Sāṃkhyasaṅgrahaḥ, Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series 50, Varanasi 1920; GRETIL e-text
